drainage.local_h: Why water sits in Marshall yards, and what we do about it
local: Marshall's sandy topsoil soaks up rain fast, then the water hits red clay a foot or so down and stops. From there it spreads sideways and settles in low corners and against the foundation. That is why a yard can be bone dry on top an hour after a storm and still have a soft, wet strip along the back wall. The fix starts with where the water is coming from, not with a trench.

Older Marshall homes add problems of their own. Downspouts empty into flower beds right at the wall. Yards settle over decades and the grade that once sloped away now slopes in. Patios and walks were poured without an outlet. We often start with the cheap fixes: extending or rerouting downspouts in solid pipe, regrading, a swale or a pop-up emitter. Many yards never need a French drain. Whichever fix fits, the written estimate says what we are installing and why.

When a French drain is the answer, we walk the property during or right after a rain when we can and trace where the water comes from and where it sits. The trench runs with a steady fall to a real outlet: daylight, a curb, a lower part of the lot or an emitter. Pipe is sock-wrapped and backfilled with #57 stone so clay fines cannot clog it. Cheap corrugated pipe laid shallow with no outlet silts up in a season or two.

Small fixes run $450 to $1,000. A standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000, a full system $3,000 to $4,500, and large or combined jobs start at $4,500. Linear feet, dig depth, outlet distance and the finish on top all count. We cap the trench with soil and sod or finish it in river rock or a dry creek bed. Getting it done before spring rains means one less season with a pond in the corner.

faq.q: Why is there water along the back of my Marshall house?
faq.a: Usually rain is soaking into the sandy topsoil, hitting clay and spreading sideways toward the foundation. A downspout emptying at the wall or a yard that has settled toward the house makes it worse. We trace the water on the walkthrough and pick the simplest fix that works.

faq.q: How much does drainage work cost in Marshall?
faq.a: Small fixes such as rerouting a downspout or draining one low spot run $450 to $1,000. A standard single French drain run is $1,900 to $3,000, full systems run $3,000 to $4,500, and large jobs go past $4,500. Most projects land between $2,000 and $3,750.

faq.q: Do I need a French drain or something simpler?
faq.a: Often something simpler. Downspout extensions, regrading, a swale or a pop-up emitter solve many problems for far less. A French drain is the answer when water has to be intercepted and carried to an outlet. The written estimate says what we are installing and why.

faq.q: Where does the water go once it is in the drain?
faq.a: To a real outlet. That may be daylight at a lower part of the lot, a curb or a pop-up emitter. A drain without an outlet just becomes an underground pond. We set the pipe with a steady fall toward that outlet before we build the rest.

faq.q: When is the best time to look at a drainage problem?
faq.a: During or right after a rain, when you can see where the water goes. We fix drainage year-round, and digging goes faster in a dry stretch when the clay is not saturated. If you can, take a photo or video of the problem during a storm and send it with your request.

fertilization.local_h: Feeding a Marshall lawn on the right dates, not the store's
local: Soil in Harrison County does not warm to 65 degrees until about mid-April, which is why we skip March no matter what the garden aisle says. Fertilizer put down that early mostly washes out with the next rain, because the grass is still half asleep. Our first Marshall feeding goes down around late April, once nights hold above 60. Early July brings the second, a summer-safe feeding, and early September builds roots before dormancy.

Many Marshall lawns grow in the shade of old oaks and pecans, and shaded St. Augustine needs a lighter hand than open bermuda. Push heavy nitrogen into grass that is short on sun and you mostly grow soft, floppy blades. So the plan follows the light: more for sunny bermuda on the edge of town, less under the canopy. We check the grass type and the shade on the walkthrough and put the plan in writing.

The October visit is the one people misread. Late nitrogen pushes growth the first frost burns off, and on St. Augustine it can feed large patch, a fungus that wakes up when fall nights cool and the grass stays damp. So the last real nitrogen goes down in early September. October is a low-nitrogen, potassium-heavy winterizer for rooting and cold hardiness. Add a wet leaf mat from the big trees and the risk climbs, which is why we pair feeding with leaf cleanup.

The soil test decides the rest. Pine needles and acidic rain leave a lot of East Texas ground a little low on pH, so where the number comes back low we add lime. Compacted lawns get core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. We do not apply weed, insect or disease products. The program is fertilizer, testing, lime, aeration and the winterizer, and it starts from about $190 a visit.

faq.q: When does the first fertilizer go down in Marshall?
faq.a: Around late April, once nights hold above 60 degrees and the grass is fully awake. March is too early, since the soil has not warmed and the feeding washes out. After that the schedule runs early July, early September and a late October winterizer.

faq.q: How much does fertilizing cost in Marshall?
faq.a: Visits start from about $190. A seasonal program is priced on your lawn size, the grass type and how many rounds it needs, and lime or core aeration adds to it when the lawn calls for them. You get the plan and the price in writing before the first application.

faq.q: Do you test the soil first?
faq.a: Yes. We pull a soil sample on the walkthrough so the plan is built on numbers, not guesses. The result tells us whether the pH is low enough to need lime and which nutrients the lawn is short on. Next year's plan gets adjusted from what the lawn and the test showed.

faq.q: Does your program treat weeds or bugs?
faq.a: No. We do not apply weed, insect or disease products of any kind. What we do is keep the grass fed and well rooted: soil testing, fertilizer, lime when the test calls for it, core aeration and the fall winterizer. If you want a lawn treated for pests, that is a job for a pest control company.

faq.q: Does a shaded lawn under my oaks need less fertilizer?
faq.a: Usually a lighter hand, yes. St. Augustine getting four to six hours of light cannot use as much nitrogen as grass in full sun, and extra just grows soft blades. Under the deepest shade no feeding fixes the light problem, and we will tell you if a shade bed makes more sense.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Planting beds under Marshall's old trees
local: A bed under a mature Marshall oak or pecan is a fight over water and light. The roots run just under the surface, and the canopy overhead takes most of the sun. We amend the soil with compost without chopping through big roots, and we pick plants that can take the competition. On the walkthrough we check how many hours of sun the bed actually gets, how it drains after rain, and what you want to see from the street and the porch.

In the sunnier spots, toward the edges of town and on open lots, we lean on knockout roses, salvia, lantana and plumbago. They hold color through August, when petunias and impatiens are long gone. Annual vinca likes the heat but should wait until the soil is truly warm, usually mid-May and later, because a cool, wet spring rots it. Most of these hate wet feet, so beds are built to drain.

Where a bed gets morning sun and afternoon shade, azaleas and hydrangeas are the backbone of an East Texas planting and fit the age of many Marshall homes. In deep shade we use ferns and other shade plants rather than forcing flowers. Planting a bed to the light it has is what separates one that fills in from one that gets replaced next spring. Shrubs and perennials go in best in fall, from September through November.

Every bed gets a clean cut edge in stone, steel or a natural cut, weeds pulled by the root, and a mulch finish at an inch to an inch and a half, not the three inches the bag calculators suggest. We never put fabric under the mulch. Then we walk you through watering: deep and less often, because daily watering in clay is how good plants get drowned. If you want to see the bed drawn first, the $199 Flower Bed Preview does that.

faq.q: What flowers do well in a shady Marshall bed?
faq.a: Azaleas and hydrangeas, as long as they get morning sun and afternoon shade. Under deep shade, we use ferns and other shade plants instead of fighting for blooms. We match the plant list to the light the bed really gets, which we measure on the walkthrough, not guess from the street.

faq.q: How much does a new flower bed cost in Marshall?
faq.a: New beds fall under our planting work, where most projects run $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. Bed size and count, plant sizes, edging material, soil prep and mulch all move the price. The walkthrough is free.

faq.q: Which flowers survive a Marshall July?
faq.a: In full sun, lantana, salvia, plumbago, annual vinca and knockout roses hold color through July and August. All want sun and good drainage and hate overwatering. Spring annuals like petunias and impatiens look great in April and are crispy by the Fourth of July.

faq.q: Can you plant a bed near big tree roots?
faq.a: Usually, if we plan for it. We keep digging away from the main roots near the trunk, work compost into the top of the soil and choose plants that tolerate root competition. If a layout would mean cutting large roots, we tell you and suggest another.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under flower beds?
faq.a: No. Mulch breaks down into soil every year, and on top of fabric that soil becomes a seed bed. Weeds root through the sheet and you end up tearing out shredded fabric by year three. We edge the bed clean, prep it well and mulch at an inch to an inch and a half.

Most patio failures here come from the dirt, not the stone. Marshall sits on sandy loam over red clay, and the clay swells after a heavy spring rain and shrinks in a dry August. A patio laid on a thin bed of sand will settle, rock and split. So we dig to the right depth, compact a crushed stone base and pitch the surface away from the house. Where it catches roof water, we plan drainage before the first stone.

We build paver and flagstone patios, walkways and stepping-stone paths, fire pits, seating walls and outdoor kitchens with grill stations. hedge-trimming.local_h: Boxwood borders, holly hedges and ligustrum rows in Marshall
local: Older Marshall homes tend to come with formal plantings: boxwood borders along the walk, holly foundation hedges and tall ligustrum rows on the property line. Those shrubs have been shaped for decades, and they show it. We trim by hand where the form matters, working each plant a little wider at the base than at the top so light reaches the lower branches. A hedge sheared flat and wider on top is the one that goes bare and leggy underneath.

Timing sorts out most of what goes wrong. June is the clean window for hollies and boxwoods, once the spring flush has hardened off. Azaleas get cut within a few weeks after they bloom, never later, or you take off next year's flowers. We avoid hard shearing in late fall, because tender regrowth burns brown in the first cold snap. If you keep a holly for its winter berries, we trim lighter and accept a looser shape.

Some hedges around town have simply gotten away from their owners. Where a ligustrum has grown past the second-story windows or a boxwood is bare at the bottom, we do a hard rejuvenation cut and take it back to a size it can grow into. It looks rough for a season while it fills in, and some plants take it better than others. We tell you on the walkthrough which ones will come back and which are past it.

Most jobs land between $150 and $800. A handful of foundation shrubs sits at the low end, and long rows, tall hedges and overgrown ones run higher. Tarps go down before we start, and every clipping is raked, blown out of the beds and hauled away. Most hedges want two to three trims between spring and fall, so we can put you on a recurring schedule or come back when you call. Marshall is part of our regular service area.

faq.q: Can bare-bottomed boxwoods in Marshall be brought back?
faq.a: Often. The usual cause is years of shearing that left the top wider than the base and shaded out the lower branches. We reshape with a narrower top so light gets down again. A badly overgrown plant may need a harder cut and a season to fill in, and we say so before we start.

faq.q: When is the best time to trim holly hedges in Marshall?
faq.a: Early summer, with June the cleanest window, once the spring growth has hardened off. Late-season shearing forces tender growth that the first cold snap burns brown. If you keep the holly for red winter berries, we go lighter, since a hard June cut removes part of the crop.

faq.q: How often should my hedges be trimmed?
faq.a: Two to three times between spring and fall for most hedges. Fast growers like ligustrum and photinia sit at the high end, and slower boxwoods at the low end. We set the schedule by what you have planted and how quickly it fills in, and we can keep you on a recurring trim.

faq.q: How much does hedge trimming cost in Marshall?
faq.a: Most jobs run $150 to $800. The number and size of the shrubs set the price, along with how overgrown they are, any formal shaping and how much debris leaves the yard. You get an itemized price in writing, usually within a day of the walkthrough.

irrigation.local_h: Old sprinkler systems and shaded yards in Marshall
local: Older Marshall homes often have older sprinkler systems: cracked heads, leaking valves and zones that were laid out before the trees grew in. A zone that watered open sun twenty years ago may now sit under a pecan canopy, and it soaks ground that never dries. We start by looking at the system you have and what it is doing wrong, then fix what is worth fixing. Broken heads and lines, leaking valves, dead zones, bad wiring and heads aimed at the street are all repairs we make.

Where starting over makes more sense, we design new zones by sun, shade, turf and beds, so each part of the yard gets the water it needs and nothing more. East Texas ground is sandy loam over clay. Sand takes water fast and then the clay stops it, so one long cycle floods the low corner and leaves the high side dry. Shorter cycles that let the water soak in, with zones split by slope and light, keep the whole yard even.

Shaded beds under old trees get drip, not spray. Spray heads in a bed wet the leaves, the mulch and the siding and leave the roots thirsty. Drip puts water at the roots, wastes almost none and keeps foliage dry, which matters with the fungus that shows up in a wet, warm spring. That suits the azaleas, camellias and boxwoods in so many Marshall beds, and it keeps water off the house.

Texas treats irrigation as licensed work. Ours is designed and installed under a Texas licensed irrigator, license LI0006657, who checks every system before we call it done. We pull the permit the job requires, tie in a backflow prevention device on city water, add a rain or freeze sensor to new automatic systems and program the controller for the season. Before the first hard freeze, make sure your system has a working freeze sensor or is shut off.

faq.q: Do you install sprinkler systems in Marshall?
faq.a: Yes. We install and repair sprinkler systems in Marshall and around Harrison County, under a Texas licensed irrigator, license LI0006657. We pull the permit the job requires and the irrigator checks every system. Pricing comes after a free walkthrough, with a written, itemized quote.

faq.q: Can you fix a sprinkler system you did not install?
faq.a: Yes. We repair systems we put in and systems we did not: broken heads and lines, leaking valves, zones that will not come on, bad wiring and heads aimed at the street. We also re-zone shade that used to be sun and set up a controller nobody has touched since the house was built.

faq.q: How much does a sprinkler system cost in Marshall?
faq.a: It depends on how much of the yard you want watered, how many zones that takes, whether beds need drip, your water source and pressure, and the permit. We do not publish a rate. After a free walkthrough you get a written, itemized quote, usually within a day.

faq.q: Should my flower beds be on drip or spray?
faq.a: Drip, almost always. Spray heads wet the leaves, the mulch and the house, and waste water to wind and evaporation. Drip puts water at the roots and keeps foliage dry, which helps keep fungus down in a humid spring, especially on shrubs like azaleas.

faq.q: Does a new sprinkler system need a permit?
faq.a: Many East Texas cities require one for a new system, and the rules vary by city. We check what your address requires and pull the permit before we start. A new automatic system also gets a rain or freeze sensor, and city-water systems get a backflow device.

leaf-removal.local_h: Pecans, oaks and magnolias: a long leaf season in Marshall
local: Marshall's older neighborhoods have the trees that make leaf season last. The grass matters as much as the trees. Shaded Marshall lawns are mostly St. Augustine, which stays partly green into late fall and grows from surface runners. Leave a wet mat of leaves on it all winter and you invite fungus, and the dead circles show up in March. That is why a leaf pass here is lawn care and not just tidiness. Bermuda in a sunny yard goes dormant earlier and forgives a late cleanup, but the beds still need clearing.

On a visit the crew blows leaves out of the lawn and the shrub beds onto the street or another paved surface. Then we pull up the leaf vacuum trailer and take it all in. The hose reaches back into the yard for piles the trailer cannot get close to. The vacuum shreds as it goes, about 10 to 1, so ten yards of leaves leave as one. Older Marshall beds are full of azaleas, camellias and boxwoods with leaves packed in around the base. We blow carefully around them and re-edge the bed lines the leaves buried. Magnolia leaves are stiff and leathery and break down slowly, so they are a poor fit for mowing back into the grass. The price is one flat number, quoted in writing after a free walkthrough, so a deep drop does not change the bill.

faq.q: When should I schedule leaf removal in Marshall?
faq.a: Plan on a first pass around mid-November and a second in mid-December. Lots under heavy pecan or oak canopy can need a third. Oaks keep dropping into February, so a last visit before spring green-up is worth having. Call earlier in the fall if you have St. Augustine under the trees.

faq.q: Do magnolia leaves need to be raked up?
faq.a: Usually, yes. They are thick and leathery, break down slowly and do not mulch into a lawn the way thin oak leaves do. Magnolias drop leaves on and off all year, so the fall passes catch most of it, and we can quote a storm cleanup if limbs and leaves come down together.

faq.q: Do you bag the leaves in Marshall?
faq.a: No. We blow leaves to the street or another paved surface and vacuum them into our trailer, which shreds them about 10 to 1. Nothing is bagged, nothing is mulched into your grass, and nothing is left at the curb or blown into a neighbor's yard.

faq.q: How is leaf removal priced in Marshall?
faq.a: One flat price for the job, quoted up front after a free walkthrough. Lot size, the number and type of trees, how deep the leaves are, the beds to clear and the number of passes all go into it. There are no bag fees and no hourly meter running.

faq.q: Can I mow my October leaves into the lawn instead?
faq.a: A light October drop, yes, with the deck raised a half inch and the leaves dry. The test is whether you can still see green grass afterward. When the big trees unload in November and the lawn disappears, mulching stops working and it is time to haul them off.

mulch-installation.local_h: Refreshing Marshall beds that have been mulched for years
local: Beds around older Marshall homes often carry years of mulch laid on top of mulch, piled against tree trunks and up the siding. That holds moisture against the wood and the bark, and it does the plants no good. Part of every job here is pulling that buildup back, then re-cutting the edge so the grass stays out. We look at how much of the old layer is left before we measure, so you pay for only what the beds need.

We lay fresh mulch at an inch to an inch and a half, not the three inches the online calculators ask for. That figure comes from snow country, where mulch packs down over the winter. Here, three inches sheds light rain, holds heat and moisture against stems, and gives voles cover through the winter. A 2,000 square foot bed takes about 8 yards at our depth instead of 19. We never put fabric under it.

The best window is late April through mid-May, after the spring flush and before the heat. A second runs from late September through October, when a thin top-dress goes down before the leaves drop and the first cold front comes through. Under Marshall's pecans and oaks, leaves land on top of fresh mulch all November, so we often pair a fall top-dress with a leaf pass. Magnolia leaves in a bed can wait for that visit.

Most beds run $600 to $2,400. Square footage, bed count, mulch type and how much edging and weed pulling the beds need all count, and a thin fall top-dress costs a fraction of a full install. Shredded hardwood is the standard here, and cypress, cedar or dyed black or brown are options. Azaleas, hydrangeas and boxwood have shallow roots, so we never scrape a bed to bare dirt first. The old layer is feeding them.

faq.q: How often should I re-mulch my Marshall beds?
faq.a: Most beds want a thin layer each spring. In fall, push a finger down through the mulch to the soil. If an inch is left, add an inch. Shredded hardwood breaks down in about a year, which is the point, since it feeds the soil. We keep total depth at an inch to an inch and a half.

faq.q: Why is mulch against my tree trunk a problem?
faq.a: Mulch piled on a trunk or against siding holds moisture where it can rot bark and wood. We pull it back off the trunk and the house and lay it level, tapering at the stems. A bed with years of buildup often needs some of the old layer removed before new mulch goes on.

faq.q: How much does mulching cost in Marshall?
faq.a: Most bed refreshes run $600 to $2,400. Bed square footage, the number of beds, mulch type and the edging and weed pulling needed all move the price. A fall top-dress over a layer that is still there costs less than a full install. We measure and send a written quote for free.

faq.q: What type of mulch do you recommend?
faq.a: Shredded hardwood for most beds. It looks clean and breaks down into soil. Cypress breaks down slower, cedar holds up well in our heat and humidity, and dyed black or brown gives more contrast. Pine straw is available on request. On a refresh we match what is already in the bed.

faq.q: Should I put fabric under the mulch?
faq.a: No. Fabric stops mulch from turning into soil, and the soil that builds on top of the sheet grows weeds that root right through it. We edge the bed, pull weeds by the root and mulch at the right depth instead. Fabric belongs under river rock or gravel, not under mulch.

retaining-walls.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes builds retaining walls in Marshall, coming over from our base in Longview. retaining-walls.local_h: Holding back dirt on Marshall's sloped lots
local: Walls in Marshall come up in a few predictable places: a sloped lot, a driveway cut into a bank and an old bed where the soil has washed downhill over the years. Done right, a wall turns that slope into flat, usable yard and keeps runoff off the foundation. Done wrong, it leans and bows within a few seasons. On the walkthrough we measure the grade change, find where the water comes from and work out what the wall has to hold.

Water is what pushes walls over here. The ground is sandy loam over red clay, and clay behind a wall swells when it is wet and has nowhere to go. Pressure builds until the wall leans, then bows, then cracks. So every wall gets a gravel chimney behind it and a perforated drain carried out to daylight or a pop-up emitter. That drain is the part you never see and the part that matters most.

The base is the second weak spot. Sandy loam over clay will not carry a wall set on undisturbed dirt, so we dig below grade, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level, since every row above inherits what the bottom one does. Taller walls get geogrid tied back into the hill. We build with segmental block from brands like Belgard and Pavestone, natural stone, boulders or pressure-treated timber.

If you already have a wall leaning, propping it will not hold. It almost always has a base or drainage problem, and the real fix is taking it down and building it back right, course by course. Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand, and tall walls run $20,000 and up. If a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough. A dry stretch is best for digging.

faq.q: My old wall in Marshall is leaning. Can it be saved?
faq.a: Rarely by propping it. A leaning wall nearly always failed from water behind it or a weak base. The real fix is tearing it out, digging below grade, compacting a crushed stone base and rebuilding with gravel backfill and a drain. We tell you at the walkthrough what yours needs.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in Marshall?
faq.a: Most walls run $3,000 to $19,000, and height and length move the number most. A short garden wall starts at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls run $20,000 and up. Material, digging and drainage count too. You get a written, itemized estimate before any dirt moves.

faq.q: Does a retaining wall need a drain?
faq.a: Yes. In clay it is the most important part of the build. Water trapped behind a wall builds pressure and pushes it out. Every wall we build has gravel backfill and a perforated drain that carries water to daylight or a pop-up emitter.

faq.q: What material is best for a wall on a Marshall slope?
faq.a: For most yards, segmental block. It locks together, flexes a little with the ground and goes up clean. Natural stone and boulder walls cost more and suit the right property, and pressure-treated timber fits some jobs. We recommend by slope, height and budget.

faq.q: How tall can a wall be before it needs engineering?
faq.a: Walls over about four feet usually call for engineered design and reinforcement such as geogrid. We handle the base prep, grid and drainage that taller walls need. If yours requires a stamped engineering plan, we tell you during the walkthrough, before you commit to anything.

sod-installation.local_h: Picking grass for a Marshall yard that is half shade
local: Sod in Marshall often means replacing grass that thinned out under big trees, so we map the sun before we pick anything. St. Augustine goes where the canopy lets through four to six hours of light. Bermuda wants six to eight hours of direct sun and belongs on the open lots toward the edge of town. Below about four hours, no turf lasts, and a shade bed or plain mulch is the honest answer.

Plenty of Marshall yards should be split. A sunny front lawn gets Tif419 bermuda, and the shaded back gets St. Augustine, in Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on how much shade tolerance the spot needs. Putting bermuda under a canopy because it is cheaper and tough is the mistake we see most. It thins to dirt by August however it is fed. We tell you which grass fits where before we price it.

Prep is the real job. We strip old turf and weeds to bare soil, regrade where water needs to move, till in two to three inches of compost or topsoil, then level and roll. That also covers ground dug up for a foundation or drainage repair. Fill that has not settled sinks later and leaves low spots, so we settle and level it first. Then the sod goes down with tight, staggered seams over starter fertilizer.

Bermuda goes down best from late April through August and St. Augustine from May through September. St. Augustine needs four to six weeks of roots before dormancy, so get it in by the end of September. Laid in November it sits on the ground like a rug. New sod needs a deep morning soak every day for the first two weeks, then a taper, and we leave the schedule in writing. Patch repairs cost less than a full yard.

faq.q: Which sod is right for a shaded yard in Marshall?
faq.a: St. Augustine, if the spot gets at least four to six hours of light. Bermuda needs six to eight and quits under shade. If a spot gets under about four hours, no turf lasts long, and we will tell you if a shade bed or mulch is a better use of your money than sod.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Marshall?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700. Sod is priced by the pallet, so square footage drives it, along with grass type, how much old turf comes out, grading, soil work and access for the pallets. Patch repairs cost less, and a full yard with heavy prep costs more. The quote is written.

faq.q: Can you sod over ground dug up for a repair?
faq.a: Yes. We clear out debris, settle and level the fill, work in two to three inches of compost or topsoil, and lay sod with tight, staggered seams. Loose fill that has not settled sinks later, so we take the time to get the grade right before any sod goes down.

faq.q: How often do I water new sod?
faq.a: Every morning for about the first two weeks, deep enough to soak through the sod into the soil, until the roots grab. Then taper to two deep waterings a week that finish around sunrise. Evening watering keeps the blades wet all night, which invites fungus. We leave you a written schedule.

faq.q: When is the best time to lay sod in Marshall?
faq.a: Bermuda from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September, while the ground is warm. Aim to have St. Augustine in by the end of September so it roots before dormancy. Sod laid in November has little time to grab and mostly sits there until spring.

tree-planting.local_h: Putting a tree back after Marshall loses an old one
local: A storm can take an old Marshall oak or pecan in one night, and the yard under it changes at once. Beds and grass that grew up in shade suddenly get full sun, and the plants may need to change with it. On the walkthrough we look at where the tree stood, what the light does now and how big a new tree will get, then recommend species that fit the spot instead of the first one on the nursery truck.

For long-lived shade, live oak, post oak and southern magnolia do well here if they have room. Where the ground stays wet, bald cypress and river birch handle it, and bald cypress is the tree you see all through the Caddo Lake country northeast of town. Mature size matters as much as species. A tree that wants 40 feet of spread does not belong six feet from the house, however nice it looks in the pot.

Fall is the best planting window, from September until around Thanksgiving, while soil stays warm and the air cools. A tree set in October gets close to six months of root growth before the first hundred-degree day. We dig a wide, shallow hole, set the root flare at grade, cut circling roots and backfill with native soil, never a pocket of bagged mix that holds water in clay. Planting too deep is how most new trees die here.

A container tree sits in light potting mix, and in July that ball can dry out in about a day and a half while the clay around it stays damp. That is why every planting comes with a written watering plan, and bigger installs get a check-in around the 30-day mark. We often recommend a smaller tree that roots in fast. On open ground toward Scottsville and Karnack we stake if the wind calls for it.

faq.q: What tree should replace a big one I lost in Marshall?
faq.a: It depends on the spot. Live oak, post oak and southern magnolia give long-lived shade where there is room, and bald cypress or river birch suit wetter ground. We look at light, drainage and nearby structures first, then recommend species that fit rather than guess from the street.

faq.q: When should I plant a tree in Marshall?
faq.a: Fall, from September until around Thanksgiving, is best. Soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools, so roots grow most of the winter. We plant year-round, but a spring tree needs far more watering through its first summer, and it has only about eight weeks of roots before the heat.

faq.q: Should I buy the biggest tree I can afford?
faq.a: Usually not. A smaller tree planted in October often passes a much bigger one planted the same day within a few years, because it roots in faster and skips a summer in shock. Bigger trees cost more and need more water. We size the tree to the spot and to how long you are willing to wait.

faq.q: Do you add garden soil to the planting hole?
faq.a: No. Native soil goes back in. A pocket of bagged soil in the middle of clay holds water like a bathtub and keeps roots circling inside it. We also skip fertilizer at planting, because you want the energy going into roots and not top growth.

faq.q: How much does tree planting cost in Marshall?
faq.a: We do not publish a rate, because the tree itself drives most of the cost. Species, size at planting, how many trees and how easy the spot is to reach all count. After a free walkthrough you get a written quote with the tree, the planting and the aftercare plan spelled out.

tree-shrub-care.answer: Yard Dog Landscapes prunes and shapes trees and shrubs in Marshall, working from our base in Longview. We are a family-owned, fully insured crew, and we hold a 5.0 on Google across {{REVIEWS}} reviews. We thin crepe myrtles instead of topping them, clear dead lower limbs, remove small trees and shrubs and haul off every cut. Tree and shrub care has no published price, because it swings with plant count and condition. You get a written quote after a free walkthrough.
tree-shrub-care.local_h: Timing every cut on Marshall's older plantings
local: Crepe myrtles are everywhere in Marshall, and so are topped ones, chopped to knuckles year after year. We thin them in February while they are dormant, taking out crossing and rubbing branches and limbing them up so the bark shows. A crepe myrtle blooms on new wood by itself, so topping buys nothing. Trees that were topped for years can be brought back, but it takes two or three winters, and we plan the work out and return each dormant season.

Old azaleas and camellias set next year's buds soon after they finish flowering. We prune them right after bloom, and for azaleas no later than about mid-June. Cut them in fall or winter and you take off the flowers. A 40-year-old azalea is often worth saving with the right pruning, and we would rather tell you that than sell a replacement. If you have missed the window this year, leave them alone until after next spring's bloom.

Marshall is oak country, and East Texas has oak wilt. The fungus spreads partly through beetles that are drawn to fresh sap from a pruning cut, and they are most active in spring and early summer. So we leave healthy oaks alone then and prune them in the cold months or the heat of late summer. When a storm-broken limb has to come off an oak, we cut it clean and seal the wound right away.

Beyond pruning, we clear dead lower limbs that shade the lawn, take out small trees and shrubs that died or outgrew their spot, haul off storm debris and refresh the mulch around tree bases. We do not take down large trees near a house or grind out stumps. A tree service with the right equipment does that, and we tell you so on the walkthrough. Pricing follows plant count, size and condition, and it is quoted in writing.

faq.q: Can you fix a crepe myrtle that has been topped for years?
faq.a: Yes, but it is slow. The gentle way is to work knuckle by knuckle each February, keeping the two or three strongest shoots and cutting the rest flush. After three or four winters the knuckles blend into the canopy. We plan the full recovery with you on the walkthrough.

faq.q: When should camellias and azaleas be pruned in Marshall?
faq.a: Right after they finish blooming in spring. Azaleas should be done by about mid-June, since they set next year's buds in summer. A fall or winter cut removes the flowers. If you miss the window, wait until after the next bloom rather than cutting late.

faq.q: Is it safe to prune my oak in spring?
faq.a: We avoid it. Oak wilt spreads partly through beetles drawn to fresh pruning cuts, and they are most active in spring and early summer. We prune oaks in the cold months or in the heat of late summer. A storm-broken limb is the exception, and we cut it clean and seal it right away.

faq.q: Can you take down a large tree near my house?
faq.a: No. We remove small trees and shrubs, clear dead lower limbs and haul off storm debris, but large trees near structures and grinding out stumps are jobs for a tree service with the equipment for it. We say so on the walkthrough instead of guessing at a job we should not take.

faq.q: How is tree and shrub care priced in Marshall?
faq.a: By walkthrough, not a published rate. Price depends on how many trees and shrubs you have, their size and condition, whether it is light shaping or recovery pruning, and how much comes off the property. The quote is written and itemized, usually within a day.
